title: Overviews on adverse events in pharmacological interventions
author: Elena Dorando

Introduction Background Overviews of reviews systematically compile evidence of multiple systematic reviews in order to answer questions regarding efficacy, effectiveness and safety o f health care interventions 1. Sometimes they are also called “umbrella review s”, “reviews of (systematic) reviews” or “meta -reviews”. Following Cochrane guidance, we henceforth refer to them as “overviews”. Overviews can provide support for various decision makers, including clinicians, policy makers and the patient 1. Furthermore, the data-aggregating approach of overviews can be helpful to identify rare events that otherwise would not be detected in a single systematic review or a single study. According to Cochrane, conducting an overview of multiple systematic reviews is appropriate for four reasons: First, to summarize the evidence of different intervention s for the same condition, second, to summarize the evidence for different outcomes of the same intervention and condition, or third, to summarize the evidence of the same intervention for different conditions or populations . The fourth reason for conductin g an overview is to summarize evidence regarding the prevalence of adverse effects or adverse events from multiple systematic reviews 1. We will focus our research on such overviews on adverse events and effects in a pharmacological context. An adverse event (AE) , or “adverse experience”, is defined by the WHO as “any untoward medical occurrence that may present during treatment with a medicine, but which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with this treatment ” 2. However, there are several other terms that are also used in the context of safety and potential harms of healthcare interventions. An adverse effect, for example, is defined as “a response to a medicine which is noxious and unintended, and whic h occurs at doses normally used in man” according to the WHO3. Interestingly, the term “occurring at doses normally used in man” is not employed by the European Medicines Agency. Other synonyms used are “adverse reaction” or “adverse drug reaction ”. According to the Guideline on good pharmacovigilance practices (GVP), an adverse (drug) reaction is “a response to a m edicinal product which is noxious and unintended [DIR 2001/83/EC Art 1(11) 4]. Response in this context means that a causal relationship b etween a medicinal product and an adverse event is at least a reasonable possibility (see GVP Annex IV, ICH -E2A Guideline 5)” 6. An adverse reaction, in contrast to an adverse event, is characterized by the fact that a causal relationship between a medicinal product and an occurrence is suspected . Furthermore, the term “side effect ” denotes any (adverse or beneficial) unintended effect of the drug and can be dose related or not. A toxic effect, on the other hand, is always dose related 7. It should be noted, that between 20 % and 50 % of adverse (drug) reactions are preventable, i.e. there is an underlying medication error (e.g. patient t ook the wrong dose, physician prescribed a too high dose). However, a drug frequently associated with medication errors is apparent ly not a “safe drug”. The term “complication” is usually used for adverse events or effects caused by surgical or other invasive interventions 1. In the interests of simplification , we will refer to all those terms as adverse events in the fol lowing. The non -standardized use of terms is known to be problematic in this field anyway.

While methods for conducting overview s in general have evolved in the recent years 8-12, overviews on adverse events have not yet been analyzed in detail. Objectives There are two main objectives. That is 1 ) to investigate reporting and methodological characteristics of overviews on adverse events , and 2) to summarize the evidence on adverse events from published overviews . While the first objective will aim to improve the methods of such overview in a long -term, the second objective will resemble a sco ping review. Methods Eligibility criteria Study designs We will include overviews that have systematically searched at least one database for systematic reviews. If updates of overviews have been published, we will use the most recent versio n. We will exclude protocols of overviews, and overviews which are used to inform clinical practice guidelines or health technology assessments. Language We will include overviews written in English, French or German. Publication date There will be no restrictions due to date of publication. Publication status Only published overviews will be included. Participants / Patients There are no restrictions with respect to characteristics of participants, while only human studies will be included. Interventions being studied Overviews on pharmacological intervention s (administration of one or more drugs) will be included. Outcomes It can be assumed that the vast majority of overviews (irrespective of the reason they are conducted for) will report any adverse events if reported in the included systematic reviews. Here, we are specifically interested in overviews specifically conducte d for the fourth reason (see above), that is to summarize evidence regarding the prevalence of adverse effects or adverse events from multiple systematic reviews. Therefore, we will only include overviews designed specifically to investigate adverse events.

Information sources and search strategy We will search Medline, EMBASE, and the CDSR. For our search in Medline via OVID we will use a validated search filter for overviews 13 in combination with a search filter f or adverse events 14. An outline of the search strategy developed by an information specialist (SH) can be found below. As the search strategy is based on the combination of two validated search filters, we do not feel it is necessary that the search strategy is checked by another information specialist using the PRESS guideline 15. The search strategy will be adapted to EMBASE (via Elsevier). The CDSR via Cochrane Library will be searc hed using the term “overview” in title, abstract, and keywords. In addition, we will search Epistemonikos. There will be no restrictions due to publication period , but o nly published overviews composed in English , French or German will be included. We will not search for grey literature. Search strategy Medline via Ovid: ((overview$ or review or synthesis or summary or Cochrane or analysis) and (reviews or meta-analyses or articles or umbrella)).ti. or "umbrella review".ab . or (meta -review or metareview).ti,ab. and ((ae OR co OR de).fs. OR (safe OR safety OR side effect* OR undesirable effect* OR treatment emergent OR tolerability OR toxicity OR adrs OR (adverse adj2 (effect OR effects OR reaction OR reactions OR event OR e vents OR outcome OR outcomes))).ti,ab.) Data management Microsoft Excel will be used to manage and analyze the results of our search. Selection process Titles and abstracts retrieved from the search will be screened for eligibility by one review author and those that are not considered relevant will be evaluated by a second reviewer (liberal acceleration). Afterwards, full text screening will be independently conducted by two reviewers. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or by involving a third person. Data collection process Before the actual data extraction , we will test a data extraction form using a set of 5 overviews. This form will then be modified according to the test feedback. One reviewer will extract relevant data from all included overviews and a second reviewer will verify the results. Again, discrepancies will be resolved by consensus or by consulting a third person. Data items To facilitate the comparison of the methodological characteristics of overviews of adverse events with the results of previous research on overviews in general, we will mainly follow the work of Pieper et al. 16 when selecting the methodological data to be collected. Therefore we will collect the following data from the included overviews : J ournal name, journal impact factor in the year of publication, year of publication, number of authors, country of corresponding author, registration (e.g., PROSPERO), protocol availability (as mentioned or referenced by the authors ), inclusion criteria , primary outcomes, number of databases s earched, search restrictions (language, date, publication status), selection methods, number of included studies (SRs and primary studies), type of primary studies

included in SRs, data extraction methods, quality and risk of bias assessment s of individual studies (if presented/reported in the overview), quality and risk of bias assessments of systematic reviews, strategies to deal with discordant reviews, use of terminology, update strategies, strategies for dealing with overlapping reviews, grading of evi dence, synthesis methods, analysis (qualitative vs. quantitative), presentation of results (tabular, graphical, verbatim), causality assessments/considerations, publication bias, source(s) of funding , and conflicts/declaration of interest. In addition, we will collect the following content -related data: population, disease, (group) of drugs, route of administration, and all effect estimates of adverse events. These data will in particular inform the second objective. Quality assessment There is currently no tool to assess the methodological quality/risk of bias of overviews. However, w e will use the PRIO ( Preferred reporting items for overviews of systematic reviews) checklist 9 that was designed with a specific emphasis on harms in order to assess the reporting quality of the included overviews. Data synthesis For methodological and reporting characteristics, data will be analyzed descriptively. Data will be summarized as medians and interquartile ranges for continuous outcomes and as frequencies for categorical items. We will present data as extracted from the overviews without re -analyzing data from overviews, SRs or trials. The presentation of outcome data will be decided depending on the available data. We expect the presentation of outcome data to be very heterogeneous. However, preference will be given to tables over a narrative description. Where appropriate, we will consider converting effect estimates to facilitate the interpretation of the data. Further, we will present a map of the results to meet our second objective. Again, preference will be given to tables over a narrative descripti on. Furthermore, we will divide our results into the following categories: population, intervention, and (type of) adverse event. We will leave the possibility open for additional analyses depending on our included sample of overviews. We will create a c itation matrix to assess whether overlapping SRs exist (i.e. SRs that are included in more than one overview). To guide the interpretation, we will calculate the corrected covered area (CCA ) 17. In contrast to its original intent, the CCA will not be calculated at the overview level. Discussion Our review of overviews will provide a summary of all available evidence from overviews on adverse events in pha rmacological interventions. This data should serve as an easy -front end for decision makers. Our review will also be able to guide the methodological development of overviews on adverse events that have been a rather neglected area so far. We will mainly use passive dissemination strategies. In particular, we aim to publish our findings in a methodological and a pharmacological journal, respectively. We anticipate

using the results of this review to inform the development of guidelines to conduct and report these types of overviews. References 1. Higgins JPT, Green S.
